text:
Departing IATA director general Willie Walsh began his tenure with airlines engulfed in pandemic border closures, and has continued to fight the industry’s corner as the challenges have kept coming.

It would be easy to categorise Willie Walsh’s tenure as IATA director general as having been bookended with the industry in crisis.

After all, Walsh took the helm of the airline association when the world was still beset by lockdowns and border closures, and he leaves it with the sector facing disruption in the Middle East and fuel price pain not experienced for several years.

However, while it is undoubtedly accurate to say the industry was still in crisis-mode in April 2021 when he joined IATA, Walsh does not see an industry in crisis today.

“It’s interesting because people talk about crisis, and a few people are using that word in the context of what we’re seeing today, and I keep saying, what we’re seeing today is not a crisis. Covid was a crisis. The global financial crisis back in 08-09, that was a crisis,” says Walsh.

“This year, for some airlines it clearly is a crisis,” he acknowledges. “But for the industry at large, when we’re projecting profitability at an industry level and growth at an industry level, it’s difficult to say that that’s a crisis.”

Walsh was speaking from Geneva shortly after his last annual general meeting as IATA director general in Rio de Janeiro, and before heading to India to take up a new position as chief executive of IndiGo.

But if the industry is not in crisis, it is certainly feeling the fallout of the Iran conflict – and the related higher fuel costs in particular. This has prompted IATA to almost halve its industry profit expectations for the year from $41 billion to $23 billion.

A big chunk of that comes from Middle East carriers, which IATA now sees losing $4.3 billion rather than the near $7 billion profit it originally projected for them. The remaining profit reduction reflects higher fuel costs. IATA estimates the global fuel bill will be around $100 billion higher this year, additional cost airlines are not expected to be able to fully recapture through increased fares.

“The carriers in the Gulf region are facing big challenges. But to their credit, I think they’re facing up to them, and in many cases overcoming them,” says Walsh. “Then you’ve got airlines in different parts of the world who were financially weak coming into an environment where fuel costs have rapidly increased. It’s certainly going to be a very tough financial period for them as they try and navigate through a period of disruption to global markets.”

“So that’s going to be a challenge,” he says. “But at an industry level, we’re still forecasting growth, and if you factor out the impact on the Middle East carriers, we’re looking at growth of three and a half percent. So that’s why I don’t label this a crisis, I label this a challenging period.”

Profit peaks

Since the heavy losses incurred during the pandemic years, the airline industry has enjoyed steady profitability – if not yet returning to the profit margins enjoyed in the last decade.

“There’s more that could be achieved,” says Walsh, noting industry net margins were running at around 4-4.5% levels prior to the surge in fuel costs.

“At an industry level, we struggle to get above 5% [net margin]. But that’s not to say we can’t get above 5%,” he says. “I remain optimistic for the industry, and I think there is more certainly that we can do, and more that the industry would want to do.”

He adds: “I think it does genuinely shock people when I explain the underlying profitability of the industry versus the top line revenue growth of the industry, and then in the current environment, obviously what we’ve seen is a lot of disruption to airspace and geopolitical issues.

“Geopolitical issues have always been there, but I’ve never seen such an extensive range of various geopolitical issues impacting on the industry, and that’s clearly tempered the appetite for growth, because it is more challenging to operate in the current environment,” Walsh says.

He flags the effect of airspace restrictions over Russia impacting costs for European and Asian carriers serving those markets, and now added complexity around airspace over parts of the Middle East.

Source: IATA

“Geopolitics is definitely having a big impact on the industry and more than I’ve witnessed in my previous 45 years in the industry,” he says. “And I think that’s likely to be a more permanent feature. My experience is when we have these geopolitical issues, they never completely disappear. They ease, but don’t disappear, and I think that’s likely to be the case going forward.”

One global trend airlines have had to contend with over recent years is increased protectionism and moves away from globalisation by some states.

“I haven’t seen as big an impact as I might have expected to see as a result of that shift in globalisation, or against globalisation,” Walsh says. “We see cargo demand has been pretty good and continues to be so through that period. Our contribution to global trade continues to be very significant. So, it’s not had quite the impact that I think we worried about back then.

“Our industry has demonstrated resilience. Look at the introduction of tariffs and the speed with which the industry shifted capacity around to match the change in cargo flows,” he observes, citing the way reduced demand from Asia to North America was in part offset by significant freight growth from Asia into Europe.

Net zero challenge

Addressing the industry’s climate impact has been a central part of the mission during Walsh’s time at IATA – a challenge he has described as ‘existential’ for the industry. But after first securing IATA member support in 2021 and then a landmark resolution within ICAO in 2022 to target net zero carbon emissions for international flights by 2050, progress towards achieving that goal has been slow – particularly around development of the sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) on which much of the industry’s decarbonisation hopes are pinned.

“We argued from the very beginning that for the industry to achieve net zero in 2050 it would require everybody contributing and that it couldn’t just be left to the airlines,” says Walsh.

“The reason I was ringing the alarm bell in Rio [at the AGM] is we’re not seeing sufficient progress. People aren’t playing their part to get us there. Everybody that committed to net zero is standing back, continuing to believe that it can be achieved by the airlines.

“Airlines can’t do it on their own,” he adds. “We need everybody to play their part. If we’re serious about this, we’ve got to take an urgent review of where we are, what measures are in place and what measures should be in place.”

In this context, Walsh directs particular ire at the OEMs, energy companies and governments.

“Our gross emissions are higher than they should be because the OEMs have not been delivering aircraft. Therefore, we’re operating older aircraft and we’re not seeing the traditional improvement in fuel efficiency,” he says.

“Fuel manufacturers have not played their part, because they’re not producing SAF. All of the big fuel companies who’d make big commitments around net zero and commitments to producing sustainable fuels have all backed away from that. [And] air traffic management reform hasn’t happened.

“So there’s three critical components that have not played their part and are way behind where they should be. All of those have contributed to higher gross emissions, making the challenge to get to net zero bigger.”

The lack of progress on developing SAF is a particular frustration, given it is allied to policies in Europe which mandate its use.

“We’re just seeing very, very slow progress there, and that’s because the other critical partner in this, governments, have adopted, I believe, perverse approaches to policies. They’re mandating the use of a project that doesn’t exist.

“We keep pointing out that the sequence of policy measures is very important, and the first thing you’ve got to do is you’ve got to incentivise the production of the sustainable aviation fuel,” he adds. “What they said is we’re going to mandate you use this project, and we’re going to scale up the level of the mandates, but that’s not leading to an increase in production. And I am worried that the EU thinks that they’ve done their bit.”

Walsh notes that is even more challenging when the eSAF component is added in, as the production of synthetic fuels requires high levels of renewable energy.

Source: IATA

This EU initial mandate targets of 5% SAF usage, and a sub-mandate of 0.7% of synthetic e-fuels, by 2030.

ICAO, meanwhile, has set an aspiration of cutting aviation emissions 5% by 2030.

“We were very cautious about agreeing short-term targets because we believe that it’s not a linear progression and what you need to see in the early stages is a lot of investments and policies that incentivise investment [in SAF],” he says.

“Setting this 5% target by 2030, we said at the time, there was zero possibility of getting there because we could see what was in place today and announcements being made in terms of investments and final investment [decisions]. And when you added it together, there was just no way at a global level you’d get to 5%.

“When you set a target and you don’t achieve it, people will use that against you,” he adds. “You fail to achieve them, then you undermine their credibility, and that to some degree is what happened. So, we were much more focused on the long-term goal.”

The slow start puts further pressure on the industry goal to reach net-zero emissions by 2050.

“I’m normally very optimistic about these things, but the figures speak for themselves and I think it’s only right that we call it out,” says Walsh. “Because of where we are and the rate of progress, I think getting to net zero in 2050 is going to be extremely difficult.

“I still believe it can be done, but it is extremely difficult and every day that passes, it gets more challenging.”

Supplier pain

While upscaling SAF production was always going to be a long-term effort, airlines would have hoped their investment in new aircraft would have yielded more immediate efficiency benefits. However, this has been hit by supply chain challenges that have limited aircraft deliveries and engine availability for airlines.

“The most frustrating thing is we’ve actually spent the money to get new aircraft, but they are not in service,” says Walsh. “That is, I think, a source of anger now on the part of the industry because we are getting blamed for something that is not only completely out of our of our control, but where we have paid the money.”

The supply chain impact hits both emissions and costs for airlines. In a joint report with consultancy Oliver Wyman last year, IATA estimated that having to operate older aircraft for longer was likely to incur $11.3 billion in extra cost for the industry in 2025 through additional fuel burn, maintenance and leasing costs, as well as from holding a wider inventory of surplus parts.

Walsh says frustrations over the issue have boiled over into anger, flagging that while airlines are bearing additional costs, the profits of lessors, OEMs and fuel companies have been improving.

That anger was evident during Walsh’s AGM address in Rio, in which he called on engine manufacturers to “stop gouging us and get back to making great engines that work and that last”.

Neither does Walsh see an immediate end to supply chain issues in sight. “If you talk to some airlines they will say they have fewer aircraft grounded, so that’s a measure of things getting better. But they still have aircraft grounded and they were expected to have all of those aircraft [in the air],” he says.

“It’s probably not getting worse, but I don’t think anyone would celebrate the problem is behind us.”

Industry voice

Throughout his career Walsh has never been afraid to take on a challenge or fight his corner, and his stinging criticisms from Rio illustrate how IATA under his leadership has had a punchier voice on issues.

Walsh says little has surprised him in the role, but any surprises there have been, are on the positive side.

Source: IATA

“I continue to believe governments can do a better job,” he says. “But I knew that coming into this role.

“It’s clear that we have a responsibility as an industry to be louder and maybe more blunt with some of these players so that they better understand what we believe they can do.”

IATA under Walsh has also put data at the heart of its messaging.

“We believe data is the key to good decision-making,” he says. “If governments and politicians believe that the way to address problems is to make decisions without any reference to data, then we are in big trouble. That’s why we‘ve pushed very hard at IATA to improve the quality and the richness of the data and to use the data to support the arguments that we made.”

He hopes his successor as IATA director general will continue to progress the use of data to make its case, as well as pushing to expand the reach of the association’s membership – an area where Walsh points to progress over the last five years.

“I think the value of our advocacy is significantly enhanced by the number of airlines we represent,” he says. “The number of members within IATA has increased by 109 since I joined – we have 377 today, with increased participation from the low-cost segment, and very good geographic distribution. But there are still some gaps.

“Whoever succeeds me, what I hope they will try to do is continue to make IATA relevant and attractive to members.”

Unlike his predecessors, Walsh leaves IATA to take up an executive role within the industry. He starts as chief executive of IndiGo in the coming weeks.

“It is a fantastic opportunity,” says Walsh. “It is a market that I have spoken about for many years and to have the opportunity to participate in that is too good an opportunity to say no to.

“It shows there is life after IATA,” he adds. “So hopefully when people look at the IATA director general role they see it as a stepping stone in their career rather than something that you do to end your career.”

Pandemic lessons

Much of Walsh’s early period at IATA was spent navigating the Covid pandemic and the subsequent border re-openings. With most markets now returned, at the very least, to pre-pandemic activity levels, what lessons have been learnt?

“They may not publish learnings, but I think behind the scenes people have all learned that we’re not going to be able to behave in the way we did,” he says. “I don’t think you’ll see the extreme measures that were introduced, because quite honestly, I don’t think people will accept and tolerate some of the measures that were put in place.

“And I don’t think governments can afford it. When you look at the economic impact and the costs to governments through that period, I think they’ll be very reluctant to pursue policies like that again.”

For airlines, Walsh believes it underlined the importance of speed in reacting to crises to help protect liquidity.

“The faster you respond to these crises, the more likely you are to be able to survive,” he says. “I think airlines also recognise that their ability to fall back on support from governments was significantly more limited than maybe some people had expected. Some governments did move quickly and helped their industry. A lot of governments didn’t because, to be fair, it wasn’t just the airline industry that was facing a crisis.

“I think that that will live long in the memory of airline management and reinforce the view that you have to move quickly in the face of these challenges.”

Diverse interests

Another key challenge for the industry under Walsh’s watch has been to increase female representation within the higher echelons of airline leadership.

IATA activity in this field includes its annual diversity and inclusion awards and its 25by2025 initiative, the programme it launched in 2020 to encourage airlines to commit to increasing the number of women in senior leadership positions and under-represented areas by 25% – or to a minimum of 25% – by 2025.

“I think addressing it and putting it front and centre has been helpful,” says Walsh. “It is going to take a long time to get to where we need to get to, but I am pleased we are seeing progress in that area and again it’s a case of what gets measured gets done.”

More than 200 companies had signed up to the voluntary initiative as of September last year, including 173 airlines. The most recent figures from IATA, which cover signatories for which at least one year’s data is available, showed a third had achieved both goals and a further 31% had met one of the targets.

“For me, it is not an exercise in diversity. It is an exercise in how do we secure access to talent in the future,” says Walsh. “If our industry is one that continued to be perceived as one that is totally male dominated, then we are excluding 50% of the population as potential employees in the future. That is of great concern.

“In an environment when you are competing with all other industries for talent, we need to be seen as being an attractive industry to men and to women.”

“We have made progress,” he says, but adds: “There is still a long way to go.”

text:
A European Union court has struck down a provision that excluded business aviation aircraft manufacturing from the EU Taxonomy, the bloc’s framework for classifying sustainable investments.

The General Court annulled Section 3.21 of the Climate Delegated Act, finding that the European Commission had not adequately justified the exclusion. In its reasoning, the court noted the Commission had failed to demonstrate that other transport modes constituted credible low-carbon alternatives to business aviation in all cases, and that the criterion used related to aircraft operation rather than their manufacture – the activity being regulated.

The European Business Aviation Association (EBAA) had intervened in the case in support of plaintiffs including aircraft manufacturers Dassault Aviation and Daher.

“The court’s judgment marks a significant and welcome development,” EBAA said in a statement. “It restores a more evidence-based and technology-neutral approach to sustainable finance rules.”

The ruling means business aviation aircraft manufacturers could now qualify for access to sustainable finance under the EU Taxonomy, opening up green investment channels previously unavailable to the sector.

EBAA argued the original exclusion was unjust given the sector’s track record on innovation, including more efficient aircraft design, advanced materials and lower-emission propulsion.

Business aviation operators are also participating in sustainable aviation fuel uptake under the ReFuelEU Aviation regulation.

The association said the judgment sends a broader signal that EU sustainable finance rules must remain “evidence-based, proportionate and aligned with the actual characteristics of the activity being regulated.”

Refinity has licensed a patented catalytic oligomerization process from PNNL that addresses a critical challenge in plastic waste conversion: impurity management.
"When you make olefins from mixed plastic waste, they have a lot of impurities," said Udishnu Sanyal, a chemical engineer at PNNL.

Sustainable aviation fuel and beyond Refinity plans to initially leverage the licensed process for converting plastic waste into jet fuel range liquids for sustainable aviation fuel applications.

text:
A partnership between the Department of Energy's Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) and Orlando, FL-based Refinity is poised to transform how the plastics industry handles mixed plastic waste, converting it into valuable products ranging from sustainable aviation fuel to lubricant precursors.

Refinity has licensed a patented catalytic oligomerization process from PNNL that addresses a critical challenge in plastic waste conversion: impurity management. The technology enables the company to transform postconsumer rigid and flexible packaging into industrial-grade chemicals, plastics, and fuels without extensive purification procedures that typically drive up costs and complexity.

Solving the impurity problem

Refinity's patented conversion process breaks down mixed plastic waste into light olefins — short carbon chain molecules like ethylene and propylene that serve as building blocks for numerous industrial applications. However, these molecules come with a significant drawback.

"When you make olefins from mixed plastic waste, they have a lot of impurities," said Udishnu Sanyal, a chemical engineer at PNNL. "Many industrial applications of light olefins, like fuels and plastics, are very sensitive to impurities and require clean olefin precursors. So, in order to make the olefins useful for those industries, you need to go through additional separation and clean-up procedures, which increase the cost and complexity of the process," Sanyal added.

PNNL's licensed technology offers an elegant solution. The laboratory's catalytic oligomerization process combines short carbon chains into longer, industrially useful carbon chains while simultaneously addressing impurity concerns.

Expanding feedstock flexibility

PNNL's extensive chemistry and catalysis research background proved instrumental in adapting the technology for Refinity's specific needs. While the laboratory's oligomerization work traditionally focused on specific light olefins, researchers successfully modified their approach to accommodate mixed feedstocks.

"Our catalysts would take Refinity's mixture of ethylene and propylene and convert them into pure carbon chains in the C8 – C16 range without the need for as many separation and clean-up procedures. This is perfect for making fuels," said Mond Guo, an engineer and commercialization manager at PNNL. "Now, instead of just being able to accept one feedstock material, we can accept a mixed bag of all sorts of light olefins. That opens up a ton of new feedstocks that can be effectively leveraged for conversion into valuable products."

Sustainable aviation fuel and beyond

Refinity plans to initially leverage the licensed process for converting plastic waste into jet fuel range liquids for sustainable aviation fuel applications. The company aims to demonstrate the complete conversion process — from mixed plastic waste to light olefins to distillate-range hydrocarbon liquids — by year's end.

However, the partnership's potential extends far beyond aviation fuel. "The C8 – C16 range is great for fuels," Sanyal said. "But we're also interested in working together to help Refinity achieve much narrower distributions that could enable other products: for instance, C14 to C18, which could be used to produce lubricant precursors."

Accelerating commercialization

PNNL's Office of Collaboration and Commercialization played a crucial role in facilitating the technology transfer, guiding researchers through each step of the partnership process.

"Partnerships like this demonstrate how PNNL's expertise and decades of experience in catalysis, chemical processing, and working with industry can move technologies beyond the laboratory to address real commercial opportunities," said Allan Tuan, integrated partnership team lead at PNNL. "By translating fundamental research into scalable technologies that improve efficiency, expand feedstock flexibility, and create higher-value products, we're helping companies accelerate commercialization while advancing additional manufacturing pathways."

"We are very enthusiastic about our partnership with PNNL," said Bill Grieco, Refinity's CEO. "By combining our light olefins production technology with PNNL's catalytic upgrading capabilities, we believe we can produce customized circular hydrocarbons and unlock additional value from waste plastic while expanding feedstock options for fuels and petrochemical products."

The Department of Energy's Alternative Fuels and Feedstocks Office, formerly the Bioenergy Technologies Office, supported development of PNNL's catalytic oligomerization process.

title: At VivaTech, Rice turns lab-born ideas into transatlantic partnerships
description:
From its booth in Pavilion 7, Rice introduced seven startups from its innovation ecosystem, unveiled new research partnerships with French and German institutions and reinforced the role of the Rice Global Paris Center, its hub in the French capital since 2023.

text:
When Rice University President Reginald DesRoches took the Purple Stage and Caroline Levander, the university’s vice president for global strategy, spoke at the Business Redefined Arena, the crowds they drew to VivaTech came for the same reason: to hear how a leading research university is approaching artificial intelligence.

Those talks anchored Rice’s second appearance at Europe’s largest technology event held June 17-20 at Paris Expo Porte de Versailles. Now a fixture of the European innovation calendar, the 10th anniversary of VivaTech drew startups, investors and government leaders from more than 160 countries. From its booth in Pavilion 7, Rice introduced seven startups from its innovation ecosystem, unveiled new research partnerships with French and German institutions and reinforced the role of the Rice Global Paris Center, its hub in the French capital since 2023.

“We’re focused on solving some of the most pressing global challenges and to do that we have to partner with the best talent from all over the globe, including the talent here in Paris and across Europe,” DesRoches said.

The booth gave that ambition a physical form. Throughout the week, founders fielded questions from investors, corporations and fellow researchers a few steps from the main stages. The seven companies span green hydrogen, sustainable aviation fuel, energy-efficient buildings, advanced materials, semiconductor cooling, sustainable AI and low-carbon chemistry. Rice, ranked No. 1 in the United States for graduate entrepreneurship by the Princeton Review, has supported more than 3,700 startups through the Rice Alliance, companies that have together raised more than $31 billion.

“For Rice to be here and to have a primary spot is a huge identity boost for the university and for the city of Houston,” Levander said.

The week’s marquee announcements began June 18 when DesRoches and El-Mouhoub Mouhoud, the president of Université Paris Sciences & Lettres, unveiled “Frontiers of Knowledge,” a new international symposium that builds on years of collaboration between the two universities. Its inaugural edition, set for spring 2027, will focus on the frontiers of quantum physics and technologies, with particular attention to cavity quantum electrodynamics.

Rice extended that push into materials science through the Rice-Max Planck Partnership in Quantum Materials, a collaboration with one of the continent’s most prominent research organizations.

“This marks a signal moment in our research network expansion and it happens with European leaders,” Levander said. “We are honored and privileged to call these institutions our neighbors.”

The week also delivered a measure of validation for the founders themselves. Helix Earth is commercializing NASA-derived cooling technology that co-founder and CEO Rawand Rasheed first developed during his doctoral research at Rice. At VivaTech, he announced the company would bring it back to campus.

“It was wonderful to make the announcement that we’re going to be at Rice, bringing the technology home to where it really started,” Rasheed said. “It’s a full-circle moment. We get to come back and help solve some of the problems the campus faces around humidity, which anyone in Houston knows well.”

The breadth of the ecosystem was visible across the booth. Solidec builds generators that produce essential chemicals such as hydrogen peroxide on site from air, water and electricity. HEXASpec engineers materials that draw heat away from electronic chips, a growing constraint for AI computing. MCatalysis and DirectH2, both led by cofounder Michael Irwin, turn to microwave catalysis and solar-driven panels, respectively, to make cleaner fuels and hydrogen on demand.

The startups also competed for attention on VivaTech’s stages. At the June 19 Rice Pitch Session, DexMat won the audience vote for Galvorn, the advanced carbon material the company positions as a lightweight, conductive alternative to metals such as steel.

“We’ve been inundated here with interesting corporate customers, partners and potential investors,” said DexMat CEO and Rice alum Bryan Guido Hassin. “We have a growing customer base in Europe, and this was a great chance to connect in person with people we usually only see by Zoom.”

Rice’s youngest competitor made the largest individual mark. Rising junior Sasha Ovalle won the Next Startupper Award for AssisTech SmartShower, a voice-controlled system that adapts standard showers for older adults and people with disabilities or reduced mobility. The honor carried a 5,000-euro prize and a guaranteed spot at next year’s VivaTech.

The Rice booth doubled as a stage of its own across the four days. Founders joined panels on how university research becomes deeptech, including sessions held alongside PSL, while DesRoches and Levander sat for interviews with VivaTech News about Rice’s research-driven model.

Syzygy Plasmonics co-founder and chief technology officer Suman Khatiwada, whose company is building a fully electric reactor to produce low-carbon jet fuel, was one of several Rice alumni working the booth.

“It feels like I’m doing service to my alma mater by being here, showcasing what we’re building from Rice technology,” Khatiwada said.

That is the link Rice came to Paris to strengthen, connecting Houston, the Rice Global Paris Center and Europe’s innovation community with ideas that began on campus now drawing attention from around the world.

text:
Airports are emerging as catalysts in aviation’s decarbonisation efforts, taking on a central role as “strong facilitators and enablers” of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) deployment.

The Airports Council International’s (ACI) World Airports and Sustainable Aviation Fuels Policy Brief 2026 stated that airports are already encouraging their users to procure SAF, helping move the industry closer to its net zero ambition.

“At the centre of the aviation system, airports can and are already playing an important role in facilitating and encouraging their users to procure SAF and, in doing so, contribute to moving the aviation industry forward in its ambition to decarbonise,” according to the policy brief.

The ACI emphasised that airports possess extensive convening power, enabling them to bring together airlines, regulators, and the wider public to align interests in support of cleaner energy adoption.

The report noted that sustainable aviation fuels could reduce approximately 55% of international aviation emissions, with life cycle reductions of up to 80% compared with conventional jet fuel, depending on production pathways and compliance with sustainability criteria.

The ACI explained that SAF can be distributed across the existing fuel supply chain without modification, a major advantage that lowers costs and complexity of adoption.

“Strong political commitments and a growing number of national and sub-national policies have contributed to the recent growth of the SAF market, which has doubled in production every year since 2023.

“Scenarios estimate SAF production needs between 330 and 500 Mt of SAF per annum by 2050. 1 Mt was produced in 2024, 1.9 Mt expected in 2025, and 2.4 Mt potentially expected for 2026,” the report stated.

The brief also highlighted barriers such as high SAF premiums, limited facilities, and geographic mismatches between production and demand hubs. The ACI stressed that unlocking financial resources and adopting policy frameworks are essential to de risk capital investments for SAF projects.

“The aviation sector, in coordination with the energy and financing sectors, must accelerate and ramp up the development of SAF on a global scale, to meet the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) global vision of reducing CO2 emissions in international aviation by 5% by 2030 through the use of SAF, LCAF and other aviation cleaner energies (compared to zero cleaner energy use), as agreed by the ICAO Third Conference on Aviation and Alternative Fuels (CAAF/3) in 2023 (ICAO, 2023a),” the report stated.

The report added that airports worldwide are undertaking initiatives to promote SAF, including consortia, feasibility studies, and roadmaps, reinforcing their role as conveners in the global decarbonisation agenda.

title: How Biofuels Can Energize American Agriculture - Vital by POET
authors: Kevin Burkum, CEO of U.S. Farmers and Ranchers in Action, Kevin Burkum, Ranchers in Action
description:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture projects net farm income to decline again in 2026, for the fourth consecutive year.
When expanded markets for bioenergy helped rescue American agriculture a generation ago, they did more than restore farm profitability — they drove investment, expanded capacity, and positioned U.S. agriculture as a force that could both feed and fuel the world.
A groundbreaking new study from S&P Global offers evidence that biofuels have the potential to do this again.
Agriculture’s moment: The biofuel opportunity The challenges facing American agriculture are real and urgent — but so are the opportunities.
What the research reveals: A data-driven case for biofuels The new study, “Fueling Agriculture: Biofuels as the Catalyst,” identifies three structural trends converging to create today’s agricultural crisis.
text:
American agriculture is facing a moment of reckoning. Crop yields are surging, harvests are hitting record highs, and yet the farmers and ranchers who feed this nation are struggling to keep the lights on. And it’s not getting better. The U.S. Department of Agriculture projects net farm income to decline again in 2026, for the fourth consecutive year.

This irony of abundance is playing out across rural America: the more our fields produce, the smaller producers’ profit margins become. Commodity prices have flattened; margins continue to shrink, and for many farm families, the echoes of the 1980s farm crisis are getting harder to ignore — when an estimated 300,000 farms defaulted on loans and rural communities collapsed.

The solution to these issues, then and now, may lie in biofuels. When expanded markets for bioenergy helped rescue American agriculture a generation ago, they did more than restore farm profitability — they drove investment, expanded capacity, and positioned U.S. agriculture as a force that could both feed and fuel the world.

A groundbreaking new study from S&P Global offers evidence that biofuels have the potential to do this again. It shows that closing today’s widening demand gap, accelerating energy innovation, and building markets that reward farmers for doing the demanding work of producing more with less could all be possible with biofuels.

Agriculture’s moment: The biofuel opportunity

The challenges facing American agriculture are real and urgent — but so are the opportunities. The industry possesses something no other sector can claim: the ability to address society’s most pressing challenges, all at once.

Let’s consider what a thriving, biofuel-powered agricultural economy could look like. Expanded demand for renewable fuels would help stabilize commodity prices, providing relief for lower-income consumers and communities hit hardest by food and energy cost volatility. At the same time, global biofuel output could triple by 2050, supplying a new generation of renewable products, including sustainable marine and aviation fuels that the global economy increasingly demands.

Most importantly, a robust biofuel market would unleash the kind of sustained investment that modern agriculture desperately needs — investment in precision farming, higher-yield crop varieties, and conservation practices that can boost productivity while reducing the environmental footprint of every acre farmed. According to S&P Global’s report, in a high-growth scenario, the U.S. alone has the potential to increase corn yields by approximately 1.6% annually, driving a 50% jump in production on existing cropland by 2050.

To understand the full scale of what’s possible, U.S. Farmers and Ranchers in Action and its partners commissioned a first-of-its-kind study with S&P Global to put hard numbers behind this vision. In concrete terms, the research illustrates how greater biofuel consumption could reverse the troubling decline in working farmland, accelerate the broader energy transition, and eliminate the most serious risks to the long-term food supply. The findings are striking — and for an agricultural sector searching for a path forward, they arrive at just the right time.

What the research reveals: A data-driven case for biofuels

The new study, “Fueling Agriculture: Biofuels as the Catalyst,” identifies three structural trends converging to create today’s agricultural crisis.

1) Population growth has begun to slow and is expected to reach ~0.4% by 2050.

2) Gasoline demand is declining as vehicle efficiency improves and demographics shift.

3) Agriculture yields are outpacing food and fuel demand. Farmers are producing more bushels per acre than markets can absorb.

The result is a persistent oversupply that is hurting commodity prices and pushing farm margins to the breaking point.

The study is clear about what happens without intervention (shown in Figure 1): lower prices, reduced planting areas, slower technological progress, and a significant drop in farm income. For rural communities already stretched thin, the consequences could be generational.

The research also presents a clear solution. Biofuels provide something that no other market can: scalable, sustained demand for agricultural commodities that grows alongside, rather than in competition with, food markets. The post-2005 expansion of agricultural capacity in response to U.S. biofuel policy proved the model works. Corn and soybean production surged. Farm income rose. Investment flowed into yield-enhancing technologies, processing infrastructure, and export capacity. Rural economies that had languished began to recover.

The S&P Global analysis shows that market-driven biofuel demand consistently outperforms direct government subsidies — not just in boosting farm income, but in accelerating the adoption of modern, lower-carbon farming practices like cover crops, precision nutrient management, and regenerative agriculture. When farmers are rewarded by the market for doing the right thing agronomically, innovation follows.

A new era for agriculture

The path forward is clear. Expanding biofuel demand — with higher bioethanol blends on road, to off-road solutions such as marine and sustainable aviation fuel, and beyond — can close the demand gap threatening today’s farmers. Biofuels have the potential to reignite growth in struggling farm communities, drive innovation, and expand agriculture’s capacity to feed and fuel the world — all while using fewer resources than before. The research doesn’t just make the case. It shows exactly how to get there.

As a farmer-led organization representing 700,000 farmers and ranchers, USFRA is excited about this research and the role biofuels can play in unleashing agriculture’s potential.

text:
SÃO PAULO, BRAZIL — An initiative among Bunge Global SA, energy company Petrobras and fuel distributor Vibra has produced the first sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) made from Brazilian soybeans with ISCC CORSIA PLUS Low-LUC Risk certification, the partners said.

Bunge originates and certifies the soybeans to produce vegetable oil at its crush plant in Rondonópolis. Petrobras, in turn, produces the SAF at its Duque de Caxias plant through the co-processing of this oil with a mineral-based feedstock. Vibra, through its BR Aviation business unit, is responsible for the distribution and commercialization infrastructure of the fuel for the aviation sector.

The project foresees the production and commercialization of 4,000 cubic meters of aviation fuel with 1% renewable content, a volume sufficient to supply the operation of 1,600 flights on the Rio-São Paulo air bridge. Initially offered at Galeão International Airport (GIG) in Rio de Janeiro, Vibra’s storage base has ISCC EU and ISCC CORSIA certification, guaranteeing full traceability and compliance with international sustainability criteria.

“Official data on Brazilian crops published by Conab (National Supply Company) demonstrate that the productivity gain in soybeans over the last decade has been greater than 20%, the result of extensive work in developing best practices in the field,” said Christini Kubo, director of renewable fuel solutions at Bunge in South America. “Now, through this unprecedented initiative, Bunge is pioneering in proving and certifying this reality, meeting the strictest international sustainability standards for soybeans.”

The use of SAF can help the global aviation sector meet its climate goals, driving significant demand for low-carbon renewable raw materials, the partners said. The initiative, they added, demonstrates that Brazilian soybeans have the potential to be a sustainable raw material solution on a large scale, enabling the fulfillment of local and international decarbonization mandates.

The ISCC CORSIA PLUS certification, recognized by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), is part of the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) program, created to encourage the adoption of renewable fuels in global aviation. It defines all the ESG requirements necessary to ensure that the product is sustainable.

Kubo said sustainability is the central pillar of St. Louis, Missouri, US-based Bunge’s strategy.

“Our clients are increasingly demanding in terms of sustainability, and we have proven efficient in translating these demands to our partner agricultural producers,” Kubo said. “By becoming the first crusher to supply certified soy with no documented impact on land use for SAF production, we are materializing consistent and transparent work that has developed over the years. This certification reinforces Bunge’s position as a leader in integration and innovation in the development of low-emission raw material solutions for renewable markets.”

text:
An American energy company has launched an experimental fuel-production facility in Húsavík, aiming to use Iceland’s geothermal energy to manufacture low-carbon fuels for aviation and transport.

The pilot project, developed by US-based Syntholene Energy, is focused on producing so-called e-fuels using hydrogen generated from renewable electricity. Company executives say the technology could significantly reduce both the cost and environmental impact of fuel production.

What’s the Story?

Original Source: RÚV

US firm Syntholene Energy has opened an experimental e-fuel production facility in Húsavík.

The company plans to use geothermal energy and hydrogen to produce sustainable fuels.

Icelandair has expressed interest in becoming an early customer if commercial production moves ahead.

Plans for Larger Facility

Speaking at a presentation outlining the company’s ambitions in Iceland, Syntholene chief executive Dan Sutton said the goal is to produce carbon-neutral and low-carbon fuels using hydrogen and captured carbon rather than fossil resources.

“Syntholene is producing high-energy, carbon neutral and low-carbon fuels also called e-fuels. We can produce the same kind of fossil fuels, which we now use fossil fuels to produce, but we can produce them with only hydrogen and carbon from green energy, especially from Iceland’s rich green geothermal energy,” Sutton said.

The experimental facility, located near the local utility in Húsavík, was constructed in roughly two months following years of development work. According to the company, the pilot plant cost less than USD 10 million to build.

Hydrogen is produced on site using an electrolyser before being combined with recycled carbon to create synthetic fuels. Similar technologies are being developed elsewhere, but Syntholene says its approach could make production more economical.

The company is now considering a much larger investment of around USD 200 million and hopes eventually to supply sustainable aviation fuel to the Icelandic market.

“Next time, we’re going to build a big factory, probably here. Since we can produce fuel for the market in Iceland, and possibly for Icelandair, which has hinted at wanting to be among our first customers. And possibly diesel for the freighter fleet and others here in Iceland. So there are big plans and a lot of hands are needed to make this happen,” Sutton said.

text:
Conducted at the Bio Base Europe Pilot Plant (BBEPP) in Ghent, Belgium, the demonstration showed the development of Cemvita’s bio-manufacturing platform from laboratory through to industrial demonstration scale, the company said on 28 May.

“Reaching 75,000 litres while achieving our set target metrics validates the … platform and our readiness for commercialisation,” said Moji Karimi, CEO at Cemvita.

“It [also] demonstrates that carbon-rich effluent streams like crude glycerine can become a scalable foundation for the next generation of sustainable fuels and bio-based materials.”

Prior to reaching the 75,000 litre milestone, Cemvita tested the process through multiple scale-up stages, progressing from bench-scale systems through to 2 litre, 30 litre, 1,500 litre and 15,000 litre fermentations.

While most industrial bio-oil fermentation technologies relied on traditional sugar-based feedstocks, Cemvita’s platform used crude glycerine - an industrial byproduct of biodiesel transesterification - to convert low-value carbon residuals into renewable oils, the company said.

Designed as a drop-in feedstock compatible with existing hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA) and co-processing infrastructure, Cemvita’s glycerol-based FermOil can be used to produce sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and other renewable fuels.

Cemvita uses synthetic biology to turn carbon waste into sustainable oils and inputs for sectors like aviation, agriculture, personal care and industrial manufacturing.

The company said it was in discussion with strategic partners in Brazil, the European Union (EU) and the UK regarding commercial use.

BBEPP is an independent, multi-purpose pilot facility for process development, scale-up and custom manufacturing of bio-based products and processes.

title: Aviation Fuel From Food Waste Could Cut Carbon Emissions - Modern Mechanics 24
description:
Sustainable aviation fuel(SAF) has emerged as one of the leading options for lowering the industry’s carbon footprint.
A team of researchers from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign has introduced a new approach to producing sustainable aviation fuel from food waste.
How Food Waste Becomes Sustainable Aviation Fuel The process begins with hydrothermal liquefaction, also known as HTL.
Their tests focused on a mixture containing 50% sustainable aviation fuel and 50% conventional jet fuel.
Meeting Aviation Standards and Handling Waste Streams Aviation fuel must meet strict performance and safety requirements.
text:
The aviation sector is under increasing pressure to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Air travel remains one of the hardest industries to decarbonize because aircraft require energy-dense fuels for long-distance flights. Sustainable aviation fuel(SAF) has emerged as one of the leading options for lowering the industry’s carbon footprint.

A team of researchers from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign has introduced a new approach to producing sustainable aviation fuel from food waste. Their findings were published in the journal Nature Sustainability. The study focuses on both the technical performance and economic viability of the process.

The researchers designed a system that converts discarded food into a fuel suitable for aviation. Instead of relying entirely on fossil fuels, the method uses waste materials that would otherwise be discarded. This creates an opportunity to support a circular economy while reducing environmental impacts.

How Food Waste Becomes Sustainable Aviation Fuel

The process begins with hydrothermal liquefaction, also known as HTL. This technology uses heat and pressure to convert wet organic waste into a crude oil-like substance. The process mimics the natural formation of petroleum but completes the transformation in a much shorter time.

Food waste is particularly well-suited for HTL because it contains significant amounts of organic material and moisture. Unlike some biofuel technologies, HTL does not require extensive drying before processing. This makes it attractive for handling large volumes of urban organic waste.

READ ALSO: Georgia Tech’s COBALT Turns Smartphones Into Robotic Arm Controllers for Global AI Training

After producing biocrude oil, the researchers refine it into aviation fuel. Earlier versions of the process relied on intensive catalytic treatment to improve fuel quality. The new study introduces a simpler approach that depends more heavily on distillation, a common industrial separation method.

Distillation works by heating a liquid and separating its components based on their boiling points. This technique is already widely used in petroleum refineries worldwide. By increasing the role of distillation, researchers reduced processing complexity and improved economic feasibility.

The resulting fuel does not, on its own, fully match the quality of conventional jet fuel. For this reason, researchers blend it with standard aviation fuel before use. Their tests focused on a mixture containing 50% sustainable aviation fuel and 50% conventional jet fuel.

The approach is similar to how ethanol is blended with gasoline for road vehicles. According to the research team, blending makes practical sense because producing enough SAF to completely replace fossil jet fuel remains a major challenge. Lower blend levels, such as 10% or 20%, are also expected to be feasible.

Meeting Aviation Standards and Handling Waste Streams

Aviation fuel must meet strict performance and safety requirements. The research team evaluated key fuel properties to ensure compatibility with standards established by the American Society for Testing and Materials and the Federal Aviation Administration. These standards help guarantee safe operation in aircraft engines.

The work remains at an early stage of development. Researchers are currently producing several liters of upgraded fuel in laboratory facilities. This volume is sufficient for engine testing and further evaluation.

The next phase involves testing the fuel in diesel engines before advancing to jet engine trials. These experiments will provide important information about performance under real operating conditions. Successful testing is essential before larger-scale deployment becomes possible.

READ ALSO: Scientists discover genes to grow bigger tomatoes and eggplants

One major challenge lies outside the refining process itself. Collecting food waste and transporting it for recovery remain significant logistical hurdles. Today, much of this waste ends up in landfills or wastewater treatment facilities.

The HTL process offers flexibility because it can also use treated wastewater-derived materials as feedstock. This expands the range of waste resources that can be converted into fuel. It also supports efforts to recover value from existing waste management systems.

Carbon Emissions, Costs and Future Potential

The HTL process produces a liquid byproduct known as the HTL aqueous phase (HTL-AP). This stream contains nutrients but also includes compounds that require treatment before disposal or reuse. Managing this byproduct is an important part of making the overall process sustainable.

To address the issue, researchers investigated electrochemical treatment technology. This system helps recover useful nutrients and acids from the waste stream. Recovered materials can create additional value and reduce environmental impacts.

The team analyzed three different scenarios for handling HTL-AP. One involved sending the byproduct to a centralized wastewater treatment facility. Another used electrochemical treatment, while a third explored future improvements in the technology.

Their economic analysis showed that the current electrochemical treatment significantly increases costs. Capital expenses and operating requirements nearly tripled the cost per gallon compared with the baseline approach. However, researchers expect future technological improvements to lower these costs substantially.

The study also examined environmental performance through global warming potential assessments. This measurement estimates the extent to which greenhouse gas emissions contribute to climate change. The results indicated that both the baseline process and improved future treatment systems can achieve negative carbon emissions.

WATCH ALSO: American company’s next-generation ejection seat offers a 92% survivability rate

Negative carbon emissions occur when a system removes or offsets more carbon than it releases. This outcome strengthens the environmental case for converting waste into fuel. It also aligns with broader efforts to reduce emissions from transportation and waste management sectors.

The aviation industry is seeking scalable fuel alternatives that are compatible with existing infrastructure and aircraft designs. Sustainable aviation fuel is widely viewed as one of the most practical near-term solutions. Technologies that use food waste offer an additional advantage by addressing two environmental challenges simultaneously.

MAIRE has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Kazakhstan’s sovereign wealth fund, Samruk-Kazyna, and the Italo-Kazakh Trade Association (ACIK) to explore the development of a Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) production platform in Kazakhstan.

The partnership will leverage Nextchem’s technology portfolio and expertise, along with MAIRE Group’s execution capabilities, to assess the feasibility of producing SAF in the country.

Focus on HEFA-Based SAF Production

The initiative will evaluate the potential for SAF production using Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA) feedstocks available in Kazakhstan. Through this collaboration, the partners aim to support Kazakhstan’s ambition of becoming a regional hub for sustainable aviation fuel.

In addition, the parties will examine infrastructure requirements, engage with key stakeholders, and define a suitable investment framework to support the project’s development.

Nextchem to Lead Technology and Feasibility Assessments

As part of the agreement, Nextchem will identify and advance key technology pathways for the proposed SAF platform. The company will also assess the project’s technical, commercial, and financial viability.

Furthermore, the partners will explore investment opportunities that could potentially be structured within the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC).

Supporting Kazakhstan’s Position as a Regional SAF Hub

As per the press release, the initiative is expected to strengthen Kazakhstan’s position in the sustainable aviation fuel value chain while fostering deeper industrial and technological cooperation between Kazakhstan, Italy, and Europe.

The project aligns with growing global efforts to decarbonize the aviation sector and develop reliable SAF supply chains across key international transport corridors.

CEO Commentary

Alessandro Bernini, CEO of MAIRE, said the agreement marks an important step toward advancing sustainable aviation fuel production in Kazakhstan.

He noted that Kazakhstan’s strategic location along major Europe-Asia transport routes creates favorable conditions for developing SAF supply chains. According to Bernini, this presents a significant opportunity to combine industrial growth with long-term market potential.

He added that MAIRE, through Nextchem, will contribute its technological expertise to help develop efficient solutions and support Kazakhstan’s ambition to become a regional SAF hub.

description:
