text:
Global warming is happening, and although the aviation industry only accounts for about 2.5% of carbon emissions, the industry's overall impact is closer to 4%. Part of what makes aviation so hard to decarbonize, however, is that airliners rely on jet fuel because it's energy-dense, making batteries impractical. The added weight of batteries doesn't pose a real issue for cars, but electric power simply doesn't work for most flights due to the added weight and lack of power. Instead, the industry needs to seek other alternatives.

There are multiple solutions on how to reduce the environmental impact of flying, with Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) being the most prominent option. SAF is made of renewable materials and is engineered to mimic jet fuel. Currently, it's being blended with conventional fuel at ratios of up to 50%, while future engine programs are being designed to run solely on SAF. However, there are issues with integrating SAF and other industry challenges that make achieving decarbonization goals even more difficult.

The Latest Issues With SAF

The aviation industry is committed to reaching net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, an initiative led by IATA and ICAO. SAF is critical to this, as the industry aims for 65% usage of SAF worldwide by 2050. SAF is beneficial as it uses renewable materials and can cut lifecycle emissions by 80% compared to traditional jet fuel. In addition, using SAF also cuts direct emissions from aircraft engines.

However, IATA Director General Willie Walsh has expressed displeasure with current SAF production rates and has also criticized other players who are instrumental in helping the industry achieve its goals. When speaking with reporters at the IATA 2026 Annual General Meeting in Rio de Janeiro, Walsh stated,

"We're disappointed that fuel companies who committed to making the fuel available to us are not delivering on the promises that they've made, so what we've been saying is it is still possible, we believe, to achieve net zero in 2050 but it requires all of these players who were very vocal in terms of their commitment to net zero 2050 to start taking action rather than just standing there saying that they're committed to it."

Walsh states that the airlines themselves are doing their part to curb emissions. Instead, he accused oil companies of lacking interest in SAF production, while also calling out European e-SAF mandates as being unrealistic. As a whole, airlines are committed to reducing emissions, but Walsh maintains that the industry relies on several players to make it possible. Without a significant ramp-up in SAF production, the 2050 goal is looking increasingly unrealistic.

Current Constraints In SAF Production

IATA reported that in 2026, global SAF production will reach just 2.4 million tons, equal to only about 0.8% of total airline fuel use. Current production rates are quite low, and there are challenges associated with increasing SAF production rates. SAF is much more costly to produce than jet fuel, leading to higher acquisition costs. Current government mandates in Europe have increased compliance costs for airlines, but IATA argues these policies have not driven an increase in supply, and the organization is concerned about similar upcoming mandates for e-SAF.

Increasing SAF production is difficult due to material constraints. The most common method of creating SAF is the HEFA pathway, which uses oils, fats, and greases as feedstock. However, feedstock is limited, and the industry has to compete against other industries to secure it. Other methods are more expensive and have not been widely used, while developing new SAF formulas requires extensive testing and a costly certification process.

Production of SAF is currently limited, and there are significant challenges associated with scaling up production. Willie Walsh is criticizing oil companies for not investing enough to increase SAF supply, while stating that government mandates are increasing costs without boosting supply, resulting in higher airfares. Increasingly, the goal of net-zero carbon emissions by 2050 is looking unrealistic, a sentiment being expressed by climate experts and airline executives.

Where The Industry Stands With SAF

In 2021, United Airlines ran the world's first passenger flight using 100% SAF in one of the aircraft's engines, and in 2023, Virgin Atlantic operated the world's first transatlantic flight powered fully by SAF. In everyday operations, however, planes can only run on a blend consisting of at most 50% SAF. This is because SAF contains almost no aromatics, which help lubricate internal engine components. Airbus and Boeing are working to make their airliners capable of running solely on SAF, but this is still a work in progress.

The bigger challenge with SAF is the limited supply and high costs associated with acquiring it. Production costs have yet to come down, and manufacturers have been relatively unwilling to invest significant sums to reduce the cost of producing SAF. Some airlines have offered passengers the opportunity to make SAF donations to help offset costs, and carriers have also been lobbying governments for subsidies or tax incentives while supporting SAF mandates.

To solve challenges associated with SAF production, some believe that the future lies with Power-to-Liquid (PtL) SAF or e-SAF. However, these solutions are not yet available for widespread use. Ultimately, the airline industry is relying on SAF being easily available and cost-effective, yet there's no indication it will be anytime soon. But in addition to SAF, there are other challenges associated with the industry's push towards net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.

Current Issues With CORSIA

CORSIA (Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation) is an ICAO initiative to curb emissions on international flights. Airlines operating routes between two participating countries are required to track their carbon emissions and then offset them by purchasing verified carbon credits, using a 2019 baseline. Participation is currently optional, although 126 nations have committed to CORSIA, and it will be made mandatory in the second phase coming in 2027.

CORSIA was a ground-breaking plan as it's a global agreement covering the entire industry, but the challenge is that countries are now counting their own carbon emission reductions as part of the Paris Climate Agreement. Willie Walsh argues that countries need to allocate their offsets to CORSIA, and that this isn't occurring. What's more, many countries simply haven't made 'Eligible Emission Units' available to airlines, when the demand exists for airlines to buy hundreds of millions.

In his speech at the 2026 IATA AGM, Willie Walsh also criticized the European Union for pursuing its own system and undermining CORSIA. Under the EU's Emissions Trading System (ETS), airlines are required to purchase carbon allowances from a regulated carbon market, and Walsh argues that the EU is favoring its own system despite CORSIA being in place as a universal solution. Increasingly, CORSIA is viewed as an expensive and ineffective system that may ultimately fail.

A Well-Known Problem With Lesser-Known Consequences

The aviation industry is facing worldwide supply chain challenges that are affecting the delivery of new aircraft due to delays in airframe components, engines, and seats. Airlines aren't receiving new planes quickly enough, which is delaying network expansions and fleet renewals. However, another consequence is that airlines are having to fly older aircraft longer than anticipated. Planes like the Airbus A350 burn less fuel than last-generation airliners like the Boeing 777, and they emit less carbon as a result.

Aircraft manufacturers and suppliers hold an important role in helping the aviation industry achieve net-zero by 2050, yet they simply cannot build A220s, A320neos, A330neos, A350s, 737 MAXs, and 787s quickly enough. Airbus has been facing significant challenges in even maintaining its planned production rates for the A350, while the manufacturer is also facing constraints with the Pratt & Whitney engines powering the A220 and A320neo. Boeing has only begun ramping up 737 MAX production in recent years, while production of the 787 is still low.

Willie Walsh states that the worldwide average fleet age is a record 15.2 years, and that the industry is short of over 5,000 expected next-generation airliners. This is leading to higher carbon emissions, increased fuel costs, and rising maintenance costs. What's more, manufacturers are generally quite profitable, with some engine manufacturers reporting double-digit profits. Ultimately, the airlines are at the mercy of the aircraft builders and suppliers.

‍BRASÍLIA — Brazil’s National Civil Aviation Fund Management Committee approved the release of a BRL 13.56 billion (US$2.5 billion) credit package - divided into an emergency working capital fund and long-term investment loans - for Azul (AD), GOL (G3), LATAM (LA), and Abaeté (E4).

Coping with the jet fuel price increase

The first allocation, in the amount of BRL 8 billion (US$1.47 billion), is aimed at mitigating the impact of rising jet fuel prices, the Ministry of Ports and Airports reported to the aviacionline.com news outlet.

Abaeté can access up to BRL 80 million (US$14.7 million) under the first allocation, and the other carriers can access loans of up to BRL 2.5 billion (US$461 million) each.

The airlines will have a repayment window of up to 60 months at a 4% annual interest rate and a 12-month grace period.

As one of the loan conditions, companies agreed to a temporary ban on the distribution of dividends to shareholders until the loan is fully repaid.

Expansion and modernization projects

The second loan tranche in the amount of BRL 5.56 billion (US$1.02 billion) is dedicated to expansion and modernization projects.

The major Brazilian airlines - Azul (AD), GOL (G3), and LATAM (LA) - can access loans of up to BRL 1.8 billion (US$332 million) each.

The funds must be directed towards the purchase of locally produced sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), fleet expansion, pre-delivery payments, and the contracting of engine maintenance services.

The annual interest rates vary depending on the investment aim:

Ecological fuel and logistics infrastructure projects - 6.5%,

Aeronautical maintenance - 7%,

Fleet acquisitions - 7.5%.

Counter-obligation

The airlines that are willing to take a loan under the new credit line are obligated to increase their flight offerings in Legal Amazon and Northeast by 15% compared to last year, or guarantee that at least 17.5% of their annual departures are in those regions.

Carriers will have a 24-month deadline to comply with the set requirements and will have to maintain it for at least one year.

Final approval by the bank

The final approval for the release of funds is subject to financial analysis and approval by the National Economic and Social Development Bank.

The state-owned lender will assess a credit risk, carriers’ payment capacity, and the submitted guarantee prior to signing the loan contracts.

Dassault Aviation has won a major legal challenge against the European Commission after the EU General Court annulled rules that excluded private and commercial business aircraft manufacturing from Europe’s green investment taxonomy.

The judgment, delivered in Luxembourg on 24 June in Case T-77/24, Dassault Aviation v Commission, does not mean private jets have been declared environmentally friendly. However, it does mean Brussels cannot maintain a blanket exclusion that prevents the manufacture of business aircraft from being treated as a transitional activity that contributes to climate change mitigation.

For Dassault, the French manufacturer of Falcon business jets, the ruling is a significant victory in a long-running argument over whether business aviation should be shut out of sustainable finance rules or allowed to qualify when aircraft meet technical criteria around efficiency, emissions and sustainable fuel compatibility.

The case could also have wider implications for other business jet manufacturers, particularly where aircraft financing, leasing or investment reporting is linked to EU sustainable finance rules.

Dassault ruling opens door to business jet manufacturing as green investment

The EU Taxonomy Regulation was created to give investors a common framework for identifying economic activities considered environmentally sustainable. Aviation is included in that framework as a transitional sector, meaning it is difficult to decarbonise fully in the short term but can still contribute to the transition through efficiency improvements, cleaner technologies and lower emissions.

In 2023, the Commission adopted delegated rules setting technical screening criteria for aviation activities, including aircraft manufacturing. Those rules explicitly excluded aircraft intended for private or commercial business aviation from the scope of activities regarded as contributing to climate change mitigation.

Dassault challenged that exclusion, arguing that the rule was unlawful and affected its ability to present its aircraft manufacturing activity as taxonomy-aligned in sustainability reporting. The General Court agreed that Dassault had a valid interest in bringing the case, noting that the exclusion could affect its access to funding.

The EU Taxonomy does not ban the manufacture or operation of private jets, nor does it directly regulate aircraft use. Its importance lies in how banks, investors and companies classify activities for sustainable finance. Being excluded from the taxonomy can make a sector look less investable to institutions with ESG requirements.

For Dassault, the ruling reopens the possibility that the manufacture of business aircraft could be treated in the same broad framework as other aviation manufacturing activities, provided the relevant technical screening criteria are met.

Why the EU court rejected Brussels’ private jet exclusion

The General Court found that the Commission had not properly justified the exclusion.

One of the Commission’s main arguments was based on the CO2 footprint of business aircraft per passenger kilometre compared with other modes of transport. The court rejected that approach on several grounds.

First, it said other transport modes could not automatically be treated as low-carbon alternatives to business aircraft. The court pointed to the specific characteristics of business aviation, including flexibility, speed and connectivity. In practical terms, the court appears to have accepted that a train or airline service cannot always be treated as a like-for-like substitute for business aviation, particularly on routes or missions where scheduled connectivity is limited.

Second, the court said the CO2 per passenger kilometre metric related to the operation of aircraft, rather than its manufacture. That distinction is crucial because the contested economic activity was aircraft manufacturing, not private jet operation.

Third, the court said the Commission had failed to consider relevant factors, including the ability of business aircraft to operate on sustainable aviation fuel. The court also noted that the Commission had itself acknowledged that further analysis was necessary.

The result is a ruling that does not give business aviation a free pass, but does criticise the legal logic used to keep it outside the taxonomy. In effect, the court has told the Commission that it cannot exclude an entire category of aircraft manufacturing using an operational emissions metric that was not properly rooted in the taxonomy rules.

How the EU Taxonomy rules could change after Dassault’s win

The immediate legal effect is that the contested exclusion has been annulled. The Commission now has several options.

It can appeal to the Court of Justice of the European Union on points of law, with the deadline running for two months and ten days from notification of the decision. If it appeals, the case could remain live for some time.

If the Commission does not appeal, or if the judgment stands, Brussels will need to address the gap created by the annulment. That could mean revising the aviation taxonomy criteria so that business aircraft manufacturing is no longer automatically excluded.

However, that does not necessarily mean all business jet production would become taxonomy-aligned. More likely, business aircraft would need to be assessed against the same sort of technical screening criteria that apply elsewhere in aviation. These could include aircraft efficiency, certification for SAF use, replacement of older aircraft, “do no significant harm” requirements and wider environmental safeguards.

The Commission could also try to build a revised exclusion with a stronger evidential basis. But the judgment makes clear that any future approach would need to distinguish more carefully between aircraft manufacturing and aircraft operation, and between different forms of mobility rather than assuming that other transport modes are always genuine alternatives.

What Dassault’s win means for other business jet manufacturers

The ruling is most directly a win for Dassault, but the consequences are unlikely to stop there.

If business aircraft manufacturing can no longer be excluded as a category, other manufacturers may also benefit from a more open taxonomy framework. That could be particularly relevant for manufacturers developing new aircraft with efficiency improvements.

The ruling could improve the sustainable finance argument around next-generation business aircraft, particularly where manufacturers are seeking to show that newer aircraft replace older, less efficient models.

It may also matter to lenders and lessors. If a business aircraft, engine, component, retrofit or financing structure can be linked to a taxonomy-aligned activity, that could influence how aviation assets are reported within sustainable finance frameworks.

The reputational implications are just as important. Business aviation has faced intense scrutiny over its climate impact, with private jets often criticised for high emissions per passenger. The Dassault ruling gives the sector a legal and political counterargument: that manufacturing more efficient aircraft should not be dismissed simply because the aircraft serve private or business aviation markets.

The court has not settled the environmental debate over private jets. It has, however, forced the Commission to revisit how that debate is reflected in EU sustainable finance law.

For business aviation, the ruling is a rare regulatory win. For Brussels, it is a reminder that green finance rules must be legally precise as well as politically defensible.

text:
The aviation industry accounts for a large portion of global greenhouse-gas emissions.

Biobased, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) can mitigate climate impacts, but transitioning to SAF faces critical supply-chain constraints.

A research team at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign has developed a method to produce jet-grade fuel from food waste, contributing to a circular bioeconomy.

In a new paper, published in Nature Sustainability, they focus on technical and economic considerations.

In a previous study, the researchers outlined the process of developing SAF that meets aviation standards.

This study follows the same general approach, converting food waste to crude oil through hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL), a process that mimics natural formation of crude oil in a fraction of the time, and refining it with a catalyst.

“However, here we use a simpler approach with less catalytic intensity and greater focus on distillation, which is commonly used for industrial purposes,” said corresponding author Yuanhui Zhang, founder professor in the Department of Agricultural and Biological Engineering, part of the College of Agricultural, Consumer and Environmental Sciences and The Grainger College of Engineering at the University of Illinois. “This is a more economical and environmentally friendly method. But the quality of the fuel is not as good, and it needs to be mixed with regular jet fuel.”

Zhang compared this to the use of ethanol for cars—it must be blended with fossil fuel to work in car engines.

“It would be very difficult to produce enough SAF to meet industry needs, so it makes sense to take a biodiesel approach with a percentage blend,” he explained. “Our tests are based on a 50/50 blend, so it will certainly be feasible to use a 10 percent or 20 percent blend of SAF with regular fuel.”

The researchers conducted tests on key parameters to ensure their SAF product meets jet-fuel standards set by ASTM and the Federal Aviation Administration.

“We are still doing this work on a very small scale,” Zhang said. “But my lab is now set up to produce several liters of upgraded fuel, which is enough for diesel engine tests. After that, the next step will be jet engine tests.”

The biggest bottleneck in SAF production is getting the waste from disposal to reclamation and recovery, Zhang noted.

Most food waste ends up either in a landfill or a wastewater-treatment plant, where it is separated and converted into sludge.

Collecting and reusing food waste presents logistical challenges, but the HTL process enables use of treated wastewater as feedstock.

While HTL offers a promising approach to create SAF from wet waste, it leaves a toxic, nutrient-rich byproduct called HTL aqueous phase, or HTL-AP.

Zhang and his team explored ways to recover acid and nutrients from HTL-AP through electrochemical (EC) treatment.

The researchers also conducted technoeconomic and lifecycle analysis for the integrated process of upgrading the biocrude oil and treating the HTL-AP byproduct.

They developed three scenarios for the analysis: A baseline where HTL-AP was sent to a centralized wastewater treatment plant; treatment with EC technology to recover and valorize HTL-AP; and a future scenario based on improved EC technology.

Compared to the baseline scenario, using EC technology nearly tripled the cost per gallon due to higher capital and operating costs.

However, technological advances are expected to lower the EC costs, so they become equivalent to baseline in the future.

The team also evaluated global-warming potential (GWP), which indicates how much global warming is affected by CO2 emissions.

They estimated that both the baseline and the improved EC treatment would be able to achieve negative carbon emissions, leading to lower GWP.

About Honeywell Honeywell is an integrated operating company serving a broad range of industries and geographies around the world, with a portfolio that is underpinned by our Honeywell Accelerator operating system and Honeywell Forge platform.
text:
Honeywell analysis and MIT Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy modeling project annual savings of up to $225 billion in production costs for oil-based fuels, $80 billion in LNG alone, by 2050, using AI-enabled technologies

CHARLOTTE, N.C., June 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Honeywell (NASDAQ: HON), in collaboration with the MIT Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy, today released new research titled Accelerating Energy Expansion, which shows that digital and AI-enabled technologies can significantly reduce the cost of fuel production annually, citing applications across traditional oil-based fuels and LNG.

The report addresses three focus areas and the supporting policies needed to help achieve energy security and affordability: increasing energy supply, efficiently managing demand, and diversifying energy resources and feedstocks.

"Meeting the world's growing energy needs will require both investment in new technologies to broaden feedstock options and more efficient use of today's energy infrastructure," said Ken West, President and CEO of Honeywell Process Technology. "Honeywell is helping customers apply AI, automation, digital and connected solutions to help get more out of their existing assets while also increasing reliability and throughput. The MIT analysis highlights the significant cost-reduction opportunities AI-enabled technologies can unlock in fuel production, which is top of mind for consumers and policymakers alike as we navigate increasingly complex geopolitical dynamics."

"Energy demand is rising quickly, and many organizations are looking for practical ways to add power without waiting years for new generation to come online," said Jim Masso, President and CEO of Honeywell Process Automation. "On-site power generation and energy storage can help operators add capacity where it's needed most, helping to support the growing demands of AI infrastructure and reduce reliance on already stretched grids. As a result, this enables them to scale more quickly and efficiently."

Based on Honeywell analysis and modeling by the MIT Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy, key themes and findings revealed through the research include:

Digital Technologies, Including AI, Help Increase Energy Supply and Reduce Production Costs

Energy producers are increasingly using physical AI to improve efficiency, reliability and performance across existing infrastructure.

When applied to traditional oil-based fuels, AI-enabled technologies can reduce global annual production costs by up to $55 billion within five years of application, and up to $225 billion by 2050.

For LNG, global production costs could be reduced by $15 billion annually after applying AI-based technologies for five years, and up to $80 billion by 2050. If applied in the U.S. alone, for example, this could help reduce LNG prices by 1.1% by 2050; and, if applied globally, long-term LNG prices could be reduced by 4.5%.

Scaling Power for a New Era of Energy Demand Begins with Improving Existing Infrastructure

With rising electricity demand creating new challenges for energy infrastructure, improving the efficiency and performance of existing infrastructure may be one of the fastest ways to add available energy supply while enabling improved affordability and energy security as longer-term fuel generation projects are developed.

On-site energy production can help heavy energy users increase supply by adding power faster, improving reliability and supporting AI infrastructure growth. Conventional gas-turbine solutions for this purpose currently face permitting and equipment delays, making emerging technologies like fuel-cell-based systems more attractive, as they can be deployed quickly and with lower carbon emissions.

Intelligent energy storage technology can also help address energy demand and resilience through improving grid flexibility and reliability by managing periods of peak demand. By shifting energy to align with periods of high demand, battery energy storage can reduce the need for costly incremental grid and additional fuel generation investments while helping operators manage growing electricity loads more effectively.

Achieving Regional Energy Security by Diversifying Energy Resources with Alternative Fuels

Meeting rising energy demand and addressing energy security will require adding new sources, such as sustainable aviation fuel, to the energy mix at a faster rate.

Technology will play a central role in advancing regional energy security. By creating fuels from a broad range of local feedstocks, regions can make good use of abundantly available biomass, waste oils and non-edible crops for scalable fuel solutions.

Developing resilient regional energy infrastructure helps countries reduce reliance on imports and protects against geopolitical volatility.

text:
As the 1.5°C limit of the Paris Agreement soon approaches, GHG emissions need to be reduced and mitigated before undoable damage occurs.

One way that companies are working to reduce emissions is with carbon credits.

Carbon offsetting is when a company funds external carbon projects to remove, reduce or avoid GHG emissions to compensate for their own.

Carbon credits are what the company purchases in order to offset its unavoided emissions.

For each credit purchased, Climate Impact Partners (CIP) proves that one tonne of CO₂e has been avoided or sequestered out of the atmosphere.

According to the World Economic Forum (WEF), there are three types of carbon credits:

Those from reduced emissions (typically energy efficiency measures)

Removed emissions (carbon capture and planting forests)

And avoided emissions (for example refraining from cutting down rainforests).

According to WEF, nature-based solutions face a US$711bn annual funding gap through 2030.

Fortune Global 500 (FG500) research shows that 72% of FG500 companies now have at least one climate commitment.

The research shows that net zero is established as the dominant framework.

Taking place on 30 June at 4pm BST, a CIP webinar, Setting the pace: Carbon Credits and Climate Leadership in the Fortune Global 500, is set to host expertise on climate commitments and frameworks.

Carbon credits and climate change

CIP states that carbon credits enable critical finance to flow to decarbonisation projects, globally, allowing climate goals and communities to be supported.

WEF says that only about a third of the world’s largest 2,000 companies have set science-based climate targets.

According to WEF, the European Union is considering whether to reintroduce carbon credits into its climate goals.

The proposed amendment to the EU Climate Law would set a legally binding target to cut net GHG emissions by 90% by 2040, compared to 1990 levels.

XCF believes its phased production approach, combining near-term renewable diesel output with a defined transition to SAF, supports both immediate fuel supply needs and longer-term demand for non-fossil lower-carbon aviation fuels.

text:
CEVA Logistics is strengthening its controlled air capacity along critical transpacific trade lanes with a new air charter programme connecting Hanoi, Vietnam, to Chicago, alongside a renewal of its successful Wuxi, China, to Chicago route.

To optimise inbound distribution efficiency, these air charters leverage Chicago’s strategic position as one of North America’s key logistics hubs.

Shipments will be processed through CEVA’s advanced Chicago gateway. Close to the airport, the 700,000 sq ft multifunctional facility features 350,000 sq ft of dedicated freight space, an 8,000 sq ft Free Trade Zone (FTZ) and a 6,000 sq ft, dual-chamber cold storage unit.

As a Certified Cargo Screening Facility equipped with ETD, x-ray, and K-9 inspection capabilities, the gateway streamlines customs clearance and destination trucking to significantly reduce end-to-end transit times.

In line with CEVA’s commitment to sustainable logistics, customers using these transpacific routes can opt for Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and additional carbon reduction pathways through CEVA’s FORPLANET suite of logistics offerings.

Operating three times per week with a Boeing 777 full freighter, the new Hanoi-Chicago service provides same-day departure and arrival, supporting customers in the high tech, industrial, retail and e-commerce sectors.

CEVA added that the charter offers global manufacturers in Vietnam’s expanding industrial and technology clusters a dependable long-haul solution into the US market with predictable capacity, fast transit times and seamless integration into CEVA’s global network.

The charter provides pickup and cargo consolidation across multiple Vietnamese gateways—including Hanoi, Danang, and Ho Chi Minh City – supported by domestic operations teams coordinating multimodal flows, customs brokerage and transshipment activities.

Scaling capacity

The Wuxi-Chicago charter programme has returned for its second year of operation following sustained, high-volume transpacific demand.

CMA CGM Air Cargo will operate the Wuxi-Chicago charter utilising Boeing 777 freighters on a twice weekly schedule, providing up to 100 tons of capacity per flight.

This programme offers shippers an effective way to secure supply chain stability and planning reliability outside of volatile spot markets, stressed CEVA.

To maximize the route’s reach, CEVA has expanded its pickup coverage across key manufacturing and export hubs throughout China, leveraging its extensive nationwide ground network to enable multi-origin consolidation and seamless connection to the Wuxi gateway.

Loic Gay, vice president of global air and ocean operations at CEVA Logistics, said: “We continue to strategically expand our controlled air network along key transpacific trade lanes to guarantee our customers access to reliable and resilient capacity.

“The launch of our new Hanoi charter directly addresses the rapid growth of Vietnam as a desired manufacturing hub, while the return of our popular Wuxi service supports our customers’ needs for transpacific supply chain stability.

“By leveraging CMA CGM Air Cargo’s capabilities, alongside our Chicago gateway, we are delivering the end-to-end speed, security and flexibility that our customers need.”

Kuehne+Nagel has expanded its decarbonisation efforts with a new sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) agreement that will supply up to 5.2 million litres of SAF to help reduce emissions linked to Google Cloud’s air‑freight logistics.

While the SAF is not physically delivered on a one‑to‑one basis for each flight, the emissions reductions are accounted for through a recognised book‑and‑claim system. This ensures that certified SAF is purchased and used within the aviation network, delivering verifiable lifecycle carbon savings.

The agreement supports Google’s broader climate strategy, which includes reducing Scope 3 emissions across its supply chain.

For Kuehne+Nagel, it strengthens its “Sustainable Choice” programme, which aims to scale low‑carbon logistics solutions and encourage corporate customers to adopt cleaner transport options.

SAF typically delivers 60–80% lower lifecycle emissions compared with conventional jet fuel, depending on feedstock and production pathway. By securing multi‑million‑litre volumes, the partnership sends a clear signal to fuel producers that demand for waste‑based and advanced SAF is accelerating.

This collaboration also highlights a growing trend: major technology companies are increasingly scrutinising the carbon footprint of their freight movements, and logistics providers are responding with more ambitious, market‑shaping commitments.

text:
EU Court Overturns Exclusion of Private Jet Manufacturing from Green Investment List

EU Court Ruling on Sustainable Finance Taxonomy

June 24 (Reuters) - The manufacture of private jets cannot be excluded from a list of activities deemed to be environmentally sustainable, the European Union's second-highest court said on Wednesday, annulling a decision by the European Commission.

Background: Sustainable Finance Taxonomy

• The contested list, the sustainable finance taxonomy, is intended to provide investors with an overview of green investments.

Commission's 2023 Decision

• The Commission in 2023 excluded aircraft for private or commercial business aviation from the list, based on CO2 emissions per passenger kilometre compared with other modes of transport.

Legal Challenge by Dassault Aviation

• That decision was contested by French planemaker Dassault Aviation, which called it unlawful.

Court's Reasoning and Findings

Assessment of Alternative Transport Modes

• The EU's General Court said that other modes of transport could not necessarily be seen as low-carbon alternatives because private jets have specific characteristics in terms of flexibility, speed and connectivity.

CO2 Footprint Considerations

• It also said that the CO2 footprint related to the operation of aircraft, not the manufacturing of them.

Potential for Sustainable Fuel

• The court noted that the Commission had failed to take into account that private jets could be flown on sustainable fuel.

Next Steps

• The Commission can appeal the ruling within two months.

(Reporting by Bart MeijerEditing by David Goodman)

text:
In order to lessen the carbon footprint of the aviation industry, sustainable aviation fuels, or SAF, are becoming a more environmentally friendly option than traditional jet fuels [1]. Without changing the structure of the current power plant, drop-in SAF fuels can be used in place of or blended with fossil jet fuel [2]. These fuels, which can be made synthetically or from biomass, lower greenhouse gas emissions by 41% to 89% over the course of their life cycles. They have been demonstrated to cut SO₂ emissions by 92% and particulate matter emissions by 70–95% because of their low sulfur and aromatic compound content [3]. This rate can surpass 70% with the appropriate selection of raw materials and production methods based on renewable energy [4].

According to the ASTM D7566 standard, SAF includes seven fuels that have been authorized for use in aircraft [5]. By means of multi-level testing, certification under this standard certifies that the fuels, up to a specific blend level, meet the chemical and performance characteristics of conventional petroleum jet fuel [6]. SAF can be approved as DEF STAN 91–91 and ASTM D1655 turbine fuel after being certified by ASTM D7566—17 [7]. Table 1 presents the certified alternative jet fuel pathways, detailing their respective blending limits, feedstocks, and current TRL status for commercial aviation.

Future perspective

In the short and medium term, sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs) are thought to be the most practical way to lower carbon emissions in the aviation sector [5]. However, the biggest obstacles to the widespread use of these fuels are their high production costs and limited production capacity in comparison to conventional fossil fuels [2, 10]. The supply of raw materials, technological scalability, and the carbon intensity of the energy sources used in production processes are the primary factors driving up production costs [4]. However, it was emphasized that the infrastructure and logistics costs of alternative fuels such as hydrogen also pose a serious barrier to widespread use [11].

Adequate policy frameworks and intensive research and investment to lower SAF production costs are necessary to ensure economic sustainability [10]. Governments must create systems that lower the risks associated with SAF production and make funding more accessible, according to IATA. In this context, the Renewable Energy Directive II of the European Union has implemented a more favorable incentive scheme for aviation as opposed to road transportation [12].

Because electric and hydrogen-powered aircraft technologies are not yet operationally mature, SAFs are positioned as a bridge fuel in the aviation industry’s decarbonization process. SAFs stand out as a sustainable transformation tool for the sector to meet its climate goals because of their high degree of compatibility with current engine technologies and infrastructure [5, 8]. However, while SAFs offer a short- to mid-term solution, achieving full decarbonization in the long term will require a shift toward more radical alternatives such as hydrogen and electric propulsion. In this context, for such alternative fuels to be effectively integrated into aviation, current aircraft designs must be optimized in terms of energy integration, aerodynamics, and structural performance [13]. Furthermore, as the aviation industry transitions toward radical alternatives such as hydrogen and electric propulsion, adopting a systems thinking approach becomes imperative for managing the inherent design complexities and ensuring effective energy integration across the aircraft’s lifecycle [14].

In this research, the gas turbine engine’s individual components—including the compressor, combustion chamber, power turbine, high-pressure turbine, and exhaust—are modeled modularly using a 1D Thermodynamic Engine Model. This modular approach enables flexible, scalable, and rapid assembly of various engine configurations within a virtual environment. Consequently, adjustments at the component level facilitate straightforward analysis and validation of the engine’s overall performance. The model accurately simulates the physical engine’s operational characteristics and supports real-time simulation based on environmental factors such as altitude and Mach number. This capability allows for anticipating engine responses under different flight conditions, thereby enabling the evaluation of critical performance and safety decisions in a virtual setting.

Digital engine modeling and system architecture

To accurately evaluate the system-level impacts of SAF substitution, a high-fidelity, 1D thermodynamic engine model was developed within a physics-based simulation framework. Rather than relying on generic, static performance maps, the architecture explicitly interconnects the thermodynamic cycle, multi-species air–fuel mass flow, and transient mechanical power transfers. This modular approach ensures that localized fluid-thermal variations—driven by the distinct physical properties of the SPK fuels—dynamically propagate through the entire engine cycle.

The predictive model represents a PT6-class turboprop architecture, fundamentally compartmentalized into two main modules: the Gas Generator and the Propeller Dynamics Module. This topology (shown in Fig. 1) allows each subcomponent to be dynamically integrated while mathematically anchored to manufacturer specifications and validated operational boundaries:

Compressor: Evaluates the air mass flow rate, pressure ratio, and isentropic efficiency as dynamic functions of the gas generator shaft speed and variable inlet conditions.

Combustion chamber: Calculates total heat release and exit temperature by actively processing the blend-resolved Lower Heating Value (LHV) and chemical stoichiometry of the SAF blends. This is strictly coupled with the chamber’s physical volume, dynamic pressure drop, and instantaneous combustion efficiency.

High-pressure and power turbines: Resolves the mechanical power extracted and transferred to the respective shafts, accounting for isentropic expansion efficiencies based on the transient fluid states at the inlet and outlet.

Exhaust: Determines dynamic pressure recovery and kinetic energy dissipation as the gas flow exits the engine nozzle.

Propeller: Translates mechanical shaft power into aerodynamic performance utilizing manufacturer-derived data, expressing the power coefficient (Cp) and thrust coefficient (Ct), as functions of the advance ratio (J) and blade pitch angle (β).

By linking these independently modeled subcomponents within the physics-based simulation framework, the Gas Generator Model simulates the complete thermodynamic cycle—from air intake to turbine exhaust. This integrated 1D system architecture continuously calculates critical operational outputs, including torque, fuel flow rate, inter-turbine temperature (ITT), and shaft horsepower (SHP). These outputs are automatically adjusted in response to changing environmental factors.

To maximize engine performance while maintaining a strictly stable and safe operating regime, an advanced engine control algorithm developed at the ERHAM (Erciyes University Aviation Studies Application and Research Center) laboratory was integrated into the simulation framework. This algorithm incorporates a rigorous temperature control mechanism designed to prevent turbine blade overheating. As depicted in Fig. 2, the controller, functioning at elevated shaft speeds, enforces a material limit of 2565°R (approximately 1273 K), representing the absolute target turbine inlet temperature (TIT) that must not be exceeded. Furthermore, the algorithm dynamically regulates the fuel mass flow to prevent lean blow-off during rapid deceleration and strictly limits the operating envelope to ensure the engine does not cross the compressor surge line during acceleration. By precisely calculating the ultimate fuel delivery under these transient constraints, the ERHAM control algorithm averts thermal overloading and aerodynamic instability, thereby guaranteeing safe and efficient operational performance.

Model calibration and baseline validation

The predictive fidelity of the developed 1D thermodynamic engine model was evaluated through a rigorous calibration procedure against a standard Pratt & Whitney PT6 turboprop baseline. Due to its widespread integration and well-documented operational metrics [15], the PT6 architecture serves as an ideal benchmark. To isolate the engine’s mechanical and aerodynamic validity before introducing the complexities of sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs), all initial calibration procedures were strictly conducted using conventional Jet-A.

To establish a reliable comparative baseline, the engine’s geometric and operational boundaries were mapped using the industry-standard GasTurb simulation suite. This provided a high-fidelity, literature-validated dataset of steady-state performance outputs. The custom 1D simulation model was then systematically calibrated against these GasTurb-derived reference data, establishing a scientifically transparent and reproducible basis for the subsequent SAF integration.

The thermodynamic and aerodynamic validation of the simulation framework focused on comparing key performance metrics across a comprehensive operational envelope. Specifically, the baseline validation was executed at sea level—encompassing both standard-day (288.15 K) and hot-day (303.15 K) conditions to assess thermal sensitivity—as well as at elevated altitudes of 5,000 ft and 10,000 ft. As detailed in the comparative analysis (Table 2), critical operational parameters including gross thrust, output torque, and gas generator speed were systematically evaluated alongside internal thermodynamic stations (compressor inlet P1, compressor delivery P3, exhaust nozzle P7) and Exhaust Gas Temperature (EGT). The custom 1D model demonstrated robust agreement with the reference PT6 data across this entire spectrum, proving its capability to accurately track altitude-induced and thermal performance shifts prior to SAF integration.

Quantitative analysis of the baseline validation revealed exceptional predictive accuracy. The average relative deviations between the 1D model and the GasTurb reference data were strictly constrained to 3.77% for gross thrust, 4.96% for output torque, and a remarkable 0.61% for Exhaust Gas Temperature (EGT). Furthermore, the thermodynamic tracking of internal pressure stations proved highly stable, with maximum deviations constrained below 8.5%. These convergence metrics fall well within the stringent tolerance margins established in contemporary literature for high-fidelity 1D thermodynamic engine models [16, 17]. Ultimately, this comprehensive multi-point calibration ensures that the simulation framework correctly replicates the core thermo-mechanical behavior of the PT6 architecture, establishing a fully validated foundation prior to the introduction of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) blends.

Fuel characterization and blend-resolved inputs

In the simulation phase of the study, three sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs) were selected as alternatives to conventional petroleum-based Jet-A fuel: Gevo’s Alcohol-to-Jet synthetic paraffinic kerosene (ATJ-SPK), derived from microorganism-based isobutanol; Honeywell UOP’s Hydrotreated Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA-SPK), produced from camelina oil; and Fischer–Tropsch (FT-SPK). The fundamental baseline properties and production pathways of these primary fuels are explicitly detailed in Table 3.

These SAFs were mixed with Jet-A in varying proportions to produce a total of fifteen distinct blends, all strictly adhering to the maximum blending limits specified by the ASTM D7566 standard. To achieve high modeling precision and accurately capture the unique combustion kinetics and energy release profiles of these sustainable mixtures, a high-fidelity “blend-resolved” parameterization strategy was employed within the digital model. The blending ratios of all fifteen blends utilized in the simulations are detailed in Table 4.

To accurately capture the unique physical and chemical behavior of the alternative fuels, their specific thermochemical properties were explicitly integrated as foundational boundary conditions within the simulation framework. Specifically, the fundamental fluid property sub-models and combustion parameterizations were systematically redefined for each evaluated fuel. The critical physicochemical inputs driving these dynamic models—encompassing hydrocarbon composition, physical density, kinematic viscosity, thermal stability limits, and the specific Lower Heating Value (LHV)—are detailed in Table 5. By anchoring the physics-based solver to these exact fuel characteristics, the 1D model dynamically resolves inter-component responses—most notably the instantaneous combustion efficiency, dynamic pressure drop, and total thermal energy release—as a direct thermodynamic consequence of the selected fuel’s fundamental chemistry.

State-dependent emissions

To accurately resolve the emission species within the simulation framework, the fundamental combustion stoichiometry for each evaluated fuel blend was explicitly defined. The generalized stoichiometric combustion reaction with dry air, expressed in Eq. (1), was utilized to establish the theoretical fuel–air mass balances and the baseline species formation for any given hydrocarbon (\({C}_{\text{x}}{H}_{\text{y}}\)):

$$\begin{array}{c}{C}_{\text{x}}{H}_{\text{y}}{O}_{\text{z}}+\left(x+\frac{y}{4}-\frac{z}{2}\right)\left({O}_{2}+3.76{N}_{2}\right)\to xC{O}_{2}+ \frac{y}{2}{H}_{2}O+3.76 \left(x+\frac{y}{4}-\frac{z}{2}\right){N}_{2}\end{array}$$

(1)

By integrating these stoichiometric balances into the thermodynamic solver, the theoretical foundation for emission modeling is established. To accurately predict state-dependent emissions, a spatially resolved 1D combustor network (Fig. 3) was configured to replace standard homogeneous combustion assumptions. This architecture explicitly partitions the internal air flow into the pre-diffuser, primary dome, and cooling passages based on the physical PT6 geometry. For steady-state baseline calibration, the compressor delivery (Station 3) boundaries were strictly defined: a total pressure (P3) of 273.45 psi, total temperature (T3) of 1318.02°R, and a baseline fuel-to-air ratio (FAR) of 0.02 [15]. By anchoring the simulation to this detailed aerodynamic network, the solver accurately captures localized primary zone temperatures and specific cooling fractions. Consequently, upon introducing blend-resolved SAF properties, the model autonomously computes dynamic shifts in peak flame temperatures and localized equivalence ratios without relying on external empirical corrections.

To quantify emissions resulting from combustion inefficiency (CO, UHC, and soot), a robust mass partitioning approach was developed based on the chemical fate of the unburned fuel fraction. The central logic of this framework relies on the dynamic adjustment of the partitioning coefficients (α, β, γ) as a continuous function of the sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) blending ratio within the mixture.

The distribution of the unburned mass into carbon monoxide, unburned hydrocarbons, and soot for conventional Jet-A was established based on empirical data from established gas turbine literature [18]. These baseline normalized mass partitioning fractions are defined as:

$$\begin{array}{c}{\alpha}_{\text{J}\text{e}\text{t}\text{A}}=0.537 \left(CO\right), {\beta}_{\text{J}\text{e}\text{t}\text{A}}= 0.398 \left(UHC\right),{ \gamma }_{\text{J}\text{e}\text{t}\text{A}}=0.065 \left(Soot\right) \#\end{array}$$

(2)

The sum of these coefficients equals unity (∑ = 1), ensuring that the entirety of the unburned fuel mass is accounted for across these three pollutant species.

The alternative fuels evaluated (ATJ-SPK, FT-SPK, and HEFA) belong to the synthetic paraffinic kerosene (SPK) family, characterized by zero aromatic content and elevated hydrogen-to-carbon (H/C) ratios. Based on high-pressure combustion test campaigns, neat SPK fuels fundamentally exhibit an approximate 80% reduction in soot formation potential compared to conventional kerosene [19, 20]. Consequently, the baseline soot coefficient (\({\gamma}_{SAF}\) = 0.065) is explicitly reduced by 80% for the pure SAF simulations.

$$\begin{array}{c}{\gamma}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}}=0.013 \#\end{array}$$

(3)

To maintain the principle of mass conservation (\(\sum =1\)), the residual unburned mass fraction resulting from this soot suppression must be analytically redistributed to the CO and UHC phases. To isolate the primary chemical effects without introducing arbitrary combustion biases, the relative formation ratio between CO and UHC was held constant, strictly consistent with the baseline Jet-A behavior (α / β = 0.537/0.398 ≈ 1.349). By solving this mass conservation constraint, the methodology yields the following physically consistent boundary coefficients for neat SAF:

$$\begin{array}{c}{\alpha}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}}=\left(1-{\gamma}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}}\right) x \left[ \frac{{\alpha}_{\text{J}\text{e}\text{t}\text{A}}}{{\alpha}_{\text{J}\text{e}\text{t}\text{A}}+ {\beta}_{\text{J}\text{e}\text{t}\text{A}} } \right]=0.0567 \#\end{array}$$

(4)

$$\begin{array}{c}{\beta}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}}=\left(1-{\gamma}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}}\right) x \left[ \frac{{\beta}_{\text{J}\text{e}\text{t}\text{A}}}{{\alpha}_{\text{J}\text{e}\text{t}\text{A}}+ {\beta}_{\text{J}\text{e}\text{t}\text{A}} } \right]=0.420 \#\end{array}$$

(5)

This redistribution aligns with experimental observations suggesting that while aromatics suppression drastically reduces particulate matter, the unburned intermediate mass primarily shifts toward gas-phase products rather than disappearing entirely. For any given volumetric SAF fraction (\({f}_{SAF}\) ∈ [0, 1]), the instantaneous partitioning coefficients are resolved via a linear mixing rule:

$$\begin{array}{c}{\alpha}_{\text{b}\text{l}\text{e}\text{n}\text{d}}={\alpha}_{\text{J}\text{e}\text{t}\text{A}} . \left(1-{f}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}}\right)+{\alpha}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}} . {f}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}} \#\end{array}$$

(6)

$$\begin{array}{c}{\beta}_{\text{b}\text{l}\text{e}\text{n}\text{d}}={\beta}_{\text{J}\text{e}\text{t}\text{A}} . \left(1-{f}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}}\right)+{\beta}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}} . {f}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}} \#\end{array}$$

(7)

$$\begin{array}{c}{\gamma}_{\text{b}\text{l}\text{e}\text{n}\text{d}}={\gamma}_{\text{J}\text{e}\text{t}\text{A}} . \left(1-{f}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}}\right)+{\gamma}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}} . {f}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}} \#\end{array}$$

(8)

The dynamic Emission Indices (EI, expressed in g kg−1 fuel) are then extracted by coupling these coefficients with the instantaneous combustion efficiency (\({\eta}_{\text{b}}\)) computed by the physics-based solver:

$$\begin{array}{c}{EI}_{\text{C}\text{O}}={\alpha}_{\text{b}\text{l}\text{e}\text{n}\text{d}} . \left(1-{ \eta }_{\text{b}}\right) . 1000 \#\end{array}$$

(9)

$$\begin{array}{c}{EI}_{\text{U}\text{H}\text{C}}={\beta}_{\text{b}\text{l}\text{e}\text{n}\text{d}} . \left(1-{ \eta }_{\text{b}}\right) . 1000 \#\end{array}$$

(10)

$$\begin{array}{c}{EI}_{\text{S}\text{o}\text{o}\text{t}}={\gamma}_{\text{b}\text{l}\text{e}\text{n}\text{d}} . \left(1-{ \eta }_{\text{b}}\right) . 1000 \#\end{array}$$

(11)

It is acknowledged that the linear assumption for soot reduction may exhibit deviations at lower blending ratios due to synergistic chemical effects. Consequently, this methodology is adopted as a first-order engineering approximation, ensuring consistency with simplified emission models such as the FAA AEDT. However, it provides a robust framework for comparative analysis across different SPK types using a unified coefficient set. To maintain methodological consistency across all evaluated pollutants and to capture the full operational advantage of SAF substitution, these mass-based Emission Indices were subsequently translated into power-normalized specific emissions (SE, expressed in g kWh−1).

$$\begin{array}{c}{SE}_{\text{i}}={EI}_{\text{i}}. SFC \#\end{array}$$

(12)

Unlike CO, UHC, and soot, which are products of combustion inefficiency, Carbon Dioxide (CO₂) is the primary product of complete combustion. Its formation is not dictated by localized quenching or poor atomization, but rather by the fundamental stoichiometric carbon mass fraction (ω_c) of the fuel. Sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs) belonging to the SPK family inherently possess a higher hydrogen‑to‑carbon (H/C) ratio compared to conventional Jet‑A. Consequently, the baseline carbon mass fraction drops from approximately 0.860 in Jet‑A to around 0.845 in neat SAF blends [21]. To capture this chemical reduction, the specific carbon mass fraction for any given mixture is dynamically resolved using a linear volumetric blending rule:

$$\begin{array}{c}{\omega}_{\text{c},\text{b}\text{l}\text{e}\text{n}\text{d}}= {\omega}_{\text{c},\text{J}\text{e}\text{t}\text{A}} . \left(1-{f}_{\text{SAF}}\right)+{\omega}_{\text{c}, \text{S}\text{A}\text{F}} . {f}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}} \#\end{array}$$

(13)

The standard, state-dependent CO₂ Emission Index (\({EI}_{{\text{CO}}_{2}},\) in g kg−1 fuel) is then calculated by evaluating the stoichiometric conversion of this carbon mass into CO₂. This ideal limit is simultaneously penalized by the instantaneous combustion efficiency (\({\eta}_{\text{b}}\)), physically reflecting that unburned fuel mass does not fully oxidize into CO₂:

$$\begin{array}{c}{EI}_{{\text{CO}}_{2}}= \frac{ {M}_{{\text{CO}}_{2}}}{{M}_{\text{C}}} . {\omega}_{\text{c},\text{b}\text{l}\text{e}\text{n}\text{d}} . { \eta }_{\text{b}} . 1000 \#\end{array}$$

(14)

While the classical Emission Index (\({EI}_{{\text{CO}}_{2}}\), in g kg−1 fuel) only accounts for the fuel’s chemical carbon content and combustion efficiency, it does not capture the change in the total fuel mass flow required to produce a given engine power output. Since SAFs generally have a higher Lower Heating Value (LHV) than Jet‑A, the Specific Fuel Consumption (SFC, in kg kWh−1) varies with blend ratio. To include this thermodynamic effect into the emission assessment, the power‑normalized specific emission (\({SE}_{{\text{CO}}_{2}}\), in g kWh−1) is introduced. This metric is directly obtained by multiplying the chemical Emission Index by the engine’s SFC:

$$\begin{array}{c}{SE}_{{\text{CO}}_{2}}={EI}_{{\text{CO}}_{2}}. SFC \#\end{array}$$

(15)

Thermal NOx formation is fundamentally governed by the temperature-dependent Zeldovich mechanism. To analytically capture its nonlinear decay without the computational burden of real-time chemical kinetics, the NOx reduction was modeled using a simplified quadratic surrogate equation:

$$\begin{array}{c}{EI}_{\text{N}\text{O}\text{x},\text{b}\text{l}\text{e}\text{n}\text{d}}={EI}_{\text{N}\text{O}\text{x},\text{J}\text{e}\text{t}\text{A}} . \left[ 1-a . { \left({f}_{\text{SAF}}\right)}^{2} \right] \#\end{array}$$

(16)

where

\({EI}_{\text{N}\text{O}\text{x},\text{J}\text{e}\text{t}\text{A}}\) is the baseline NOx Emission Index (g kg−1 fuel) for neat Jet-A,

\({f}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}}\) is the volumetric SAF blend ratio (0 to 1),

a is a dimensionless coefficient that determines the total reduction when \({f}_{\text{S}\text{A}\text{F}}\) = 1. Consistent with the literature for SPK-class fuels, a has been empirically set to 0.10.

To ensure a fair operational comparison, this mass-based index was subsequently converted into a power-normalized specific emission (\({SE}_{\text{NOx}},\) g kWh−1) by integrating the engine’s dynamic Specific Fuel Consumption (SFC):

$$\begin{array}{c}{SE}_{\text{N}\text{O}\text{x}}={EI}_{\text{N}\text{O}\text{x},\text{b}\text{l}\text{e}\text{n}\text{d}} . SFC \#\end{array}$$

(17)

To isolate the fundamental operational impacts of SAF substitution, the turboprop engine was evaluated under a fixed fuel mass flow rate ( \(\dot{mfr}\) = 0.1025 kg s−1) at a constant governed shaft speed of 2000 RPM. This “equal-fuel” boundary condition allows for a direct quantification of how the enhanced energy density of synthetic paraffinic kerosene (SPK) translates into mechanical performance. The comparative results for neat (100%) fuel variants are summarized in Table 6.

Building upon the established theoretical maximums, the operational impacts of practical blending limits (up to 50% volumetric substitution as mandated by ASTM D7566) were analyzed. The linear mixing rules governing the thermophysical properties of the fuel blends resulted in a proportional increase in shaft power. Table 7 details the dynamic response of the engine’s mechanical power and Specific Fuel Consumption (SFC) across the intermediate SAF blending ratios (10% to 50%).

The results indicate a definitive thermodynamic advantage for all SAF variants. Driven by the higher gravimetric energy density of the SPK family, the engine autonomously achieved a steady power augmentation. Because the mechanical power output increased while maintaining a constant fuel consumption rate, the SFC exhibited a proportional improvement. This established thermodynamic “premium” dictates that for a given mission power requirement, a SAF-powered engine will inherently consume less total fuel mass.

The emission profile of the combustion process was evaluated using a constant combustion efficiency (\({\eta}_{\text{b}}\) = 0.98), ensuring that the unburned fraction remained uniform across all test points. The mass-based Emission Indices (EI, in g kg−1 fuel) for carbon monoxide (CO), unburned hydrocarbons (UHC), soot, and carbon dioxide (CO2) were calculated utilizing the blended chemical partitioning coefficients (α, β, γ).

The absence of aromatic compounds in the SPK-based fuels profoundly altered the combustion byproducts. As demonstrated in Table 8, the most significant environmental benefit was observed in the soot formation; at a 50% blend ratio, the soot Emission Index dropped by exactly 40% (from 1.30 to 0.78 g kg−1). The slight proportional increases in CO and UHC are a direct stoichiometric consequence of the shifted hydrogen-to-carbon (H/C) ratio inherent to synthetic paraffins and are consistent with high-pressure combustor literature. Furthermore, the lower carbon mass fraction (\({\omega}_{\text{c}}\)) in SAFs yielded a linear reduction in CO2 mass generation per kilogram of fuel burned.

Thermal NOx formation is fundamentally governed by the temperature-dependent Zeldovich mechanism. To analytically capture its nonlinear decay in response to SAF substitution without the immense computational burden of real-time spatial chemical kinetics, a data-driven impact assessment utilizing a surrogate model was employed. Based on the experimental baseline of the turboprop engine (\({EI}_{\text{NOx,JetA}}\) = 8.44 g kg−1), the quadratic surrogate equation predicted the emission suppression behavior, as detailed in Table 9.

The surrogate model effectively demonstrates that the reduction in thermal NOx is not strictly linear but accelerates slightly at higher blending ratios. At the maximum permissible 50% blend, the chemical NOx index is reduced to 8.23 g kg−1, reflecting the cooler flame temperatures associated with the hydrogen-rich combustion of synthetic paraffins.

To capture the true environmental impact of SAF substitution, the chemical emission reductions (EIi) must be coupled with the engine’s improved thermodynamic efficiency. By converting the mass-based indices into power-normalized specific emissions (SEi, in g kWh−1) using the engine’s dynamic SFC, the “double-benefit” phenomenon becomes explicitly quantifiable, as detailed in Table 10.

The transformation from EI to SE metrics reveals that the actual operational emissions are significantly lower than what chemical analysis alone would suggest. For instance, while the chemical NOx index (EINOx) decreased by 2.50% at a 50% blend, the power-normalized NOx emission (SENOx) decreased by 3.06%. This amplification is the direct result of the turboprop engine operating at a lower SFC. The double-benefit principle validates that integrating data-driven thermodynamic models with chemical partitioning accurately captures the holistic advantages of SAF deployment in aviation gas turbines.

title: "Advancing Carbon Dioxide Into Eco-Friendly Aviation Fuel" LG Chem Ltd. Launches ...
description:
LG Chem Ltd. is moving to produce sustainable aviation fuel (e-SAF) using carbon dioxide.
On the 24th, the company said it will carry out a technology demonstration project to convert carbon dioxide into e-SAF as part of the Ministry of Science and ICT's CCU Mega Project, which focuses on carbon capture and utilization.
LG Chem Ltd. plans to demonstrate a technology that captures carbon dioxide, reacts it with eco-friendly hydrogen, or green hydrogen, to synthesize fuel, and then converts it into e-SAF through additional refining and upgrading processes.
Compared with conventional fossil fuel-based aviation fuel, e-SAF is a next-generation eco-friendly fuel that can significantly reduce carbon emissions and is drawing attention as a key technology for achieving global carbon neutrality.
In South Korea, mandatory SAF blending will begin at 1% in 2027 and is set to rise to 7% to 10% by 2035.
text:
LG Chem Ltd. is moving to produce sustainable aviation fuel (e-SAF) using carbon dioxide. On the 24th, the company said it will carry out a technology demonstration project to convert carbon dioxide into e-SAF as part of the Ministry of Science and ICT's CCU Mega Project, which focuses on carbon capture and utilization.

LG Chem Ltd. will serve as the lead organizer of the project, which also involves Hyundai Engineering & Construction, LT Metal Co., Ltd., Procon Engineering, the Korea Institute of Science and Technology (KIST), the Institute for Advanced Engineering, the Korea Institute of Energy Research (KIER), the Korea Petroleum Quality & Distribution Authority, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST), Kunsan National University, and South Chungcheong Province. The project will run through 2030.

LG Chem Ltd. plans to demonstrate a technology that captures carbon dioxide, reacts it with eco-friendly hydrogen, or green hydrogen, to synthesize fuel, and then converts it into e-SAF through additional refining and upgrading processes. Compared with conventional fossil fuel-based aviation fuel, e-SAF is a next-generation eco-friendly fuel that can significantly reduce carbon emissions and is drawing attention as a key technology for achieving global carbon neutrality. The European Union (EU) plans to raise the SAF blending ratio to 70% by 2050. In South Korea, mandatory SAF blending will begin at 1% in 2027 and is set to rise to 7% to 10% by 2035.

text:
Faster electrification is the best way to secure lower energy bills and stronger energy security, according to the Climate Change Committee (CCC).

The government’s official climate advisers have stressed the importance of electrification, noting that electric cars and heat pumps can “put money back into people’s pockets”.

Moreover, the UK’s net-zero targets face “significant risks” unless there is faster progress in electrifying cars, heating and industry, according to the CCC’s latest progress report

The report notes that the government has closed some of the gaps to its upcoming targets and introduced more “credible” plans.

However, challenges remain in the UK’s climate strategy, including accelerating the expansion of heat pumps, cutting emissions from farms and supplying planes with “sustainable” fuels.

The CCC notes that 17% of the emissions cuts required to achieve the UK’s 2030 Paris Agreement climate target are currently not addressed by any government plans at all.

Amid political and industry pressure, the committee also says the government should “stand firm” on its climate goals, including its strategy for encouraging electric-vehicle (EV) sales.

Carbon Brief has covered the CCC’s annual progress reports in 2025, 2024, 2023, 2022, 2021 and 2020.

Overall progress

The electrification ‘prize’
